title: How noise-cancelling headphones erase sound
caption: Noise-cancelling headphones fight sound with more sound. Here's why they silence engines but not voices.

lines.text: Noise-cancelling headphones fight sound with more sound.
On the outside of each ear cup, a tiny microphone listens to the world around you.
A chip reads that noise and creates its exact mirror image, a wave flipped upside down.
Where a peak of the noise meets a dip of the anti-noise, they cancel out. Physicists call it destructive interference.
A second microphone inside the cup checks what still gets through, and the chip keeps correcting itself.
The whole loop runs nonstop, adjusting faster than you could ever notice.
This works best on steady, low sounds, like airplane engines, train rumble, or an air conditioner's hum.
Low sounds are long, slow waves, so the anti-noise has time to line up perfectly.
High, sudden sounds change too fast. By the time the chip reacts, the wave has already moved on.
That's why the ear cushions still matter. They block much of the high-pitched noise the electronics miss.
Fun fact: the idea is old. A German inventor patented it in the nineteen thirties, decades before it fit inside headphones.
And transparency mode? Same microphones, but instead of flipping the sound, they pass it through to your ears.
Follow for more everyday things, explained in about a minute.
